why_pinned_to_a_commit: A branch name moves under you. The commit sha fixes exactly these bytes.
why_the_version_moved: 1.3.0 -> 1.4.0, the second re-pin in an hour. 1.3.0 returns ZERO EVENTS on a CRLF log: '(.*)$' will not match past a carriage return, so every line fails the timestamp match, the file parses to nothing, and the engine takes its no-outgoing-damage path and says so — a true statement about a file it could not read. EverQuest runs on Windows, so CRLF is the NORMAL case and every LF log either side had tested against was the lucky one.

verified_here.note: Derived, not relayed. Content hash computed from the fetched bytes and compared to the content-addressed filename; then a four-cell matched pair, same content, only the line ending differing.
verified_here.our_own_exposure: The seam is not wired into the app, and gapAvailability already REFUSED the 1.3.0 CRLF report — measured: available false, the unavailable sentence — because every typed key was undefined. The degradation path did its job. Separately, web/src/lib/inventoryImport.ts:430 splits on /\r\n|\n|\r/ and its checked-in export fixture is genuinely CRLF (983 CR, 983 LF), so the one player-supplied file this app actually reads was never exposed.

conclusion: Strictly better and identical on the LF form. Adopted.

held_at_this_version.decision: HOLD at 1.4.0 through the ship. Ruled by the Director 2026-09-01 after measuring 1.5.0 against 1.4.0 on both line endings.
held_at_this_version.why: 1.5.0 changes NO computed value. Both bundles produce identical `measured` on crlf and lf input (19 keys each); the only difference is a fifth `coverage` key and a self-describing refusal on the path where the parser cannot read a file — a path 1.4.0 made rare by reading CRLF correctly. A third re-pin in two hours would trade a real risk (running on a pin this repo has not tested against, on ship morning) for a better error message on a path that should no longer fire.
held_at_this_version.what_unblocks_it: After the ship. Re-pin to 1.5.0 then, and take the refusal detail with it: on 1.5.0 a refusal distinguishes 'no input', 'this file was not read' and 'a genuine zero'. On 1.4.0 it distinguishes none of them, which is acceptable only because the file now reads.
held_at_this_version.the_hold_is_enforced_not_remembered: gapEngine.test.ts refuses '1.5.0' BY NAME (the 'refuses a NEWER engine' case), and the provenance hash and byte count are asserted against the vendored file. So 1.5.0 bytes cannot be dropped in without the pin also moving: the suite fails and the app degrades to its unavailable band rather than reading an untested engine. That test was written an hour before this hold existed and enforces it by accident of the version discipline, which is the kind of accident an exact-version guard is supposed to produce.
